highlights: Strategic balancing across Europe, China and Russia

frictionVectors.title: European gas leverage
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains dependent on Algerian gas while pressing for more flexible supply and energy-transition commitments. Algiers retains strong control over production but faces long-term demand uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara and Sahel exposure
frictionVectors.details: Regional tensions involving Morocco and instability across the Sahel constrain Algeria's diplomatic room and raise border-security costs.

frictionVectors.title: External control of strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is drawing strong US and European backing alongside Chinese commercial interests, making transport access to copper and cobalt a major arena of influence.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining oil output and foreign-operated production limit fiscal autonomy and expose Luanda to external capital, technology and price cycles.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity near the Burkina Faso and Niger frontiers is increasing the cost of securing northern territory and transport corridors. Benin is expanding security partnerships while trying to preserve policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Niger transit disruption
frictionVectors.details: Political tensions with Niger have disrupted established trade routes and reduced the leverage of Benin's port economy. Regional mediation and corridor diversification remain ongoing.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains substantial influence over diamond extraction and beneficiation, but weak global demand and De Beers restructuring could reduce revenues and negotiating leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral competition
frictionVectors.details: Interest in copper, nickel and other critical minerals is increasing external competition for licenses and infrastructure access. Gaborone is seeking investment without surrendering regulatory control.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector control struggle
frictionVectors.details: The junta is tightening state involvement in gold production and seeking greater value capture, but informal mining networks and insecurity limit effective oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security alignment
frictionVectors.details: Expanded security cooperation with Russia offers the regime an alternative to Western partners but may increase dependence on opaque security and mining arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals opacity
frictionVectors.details: Gold and nickel development is increasingly tied to foreign capital and opaque licensing, leaving the state with limited bargaining power and weak local value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda border tensions
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations over armed groups and border insecurity continue to disrupt regional trade and complicate Burundi's access to external security and infrastructure partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime competition
frictionVectors.details: Mindelo and Praia are being positioned as Atlantic logistics and maritime-security hubs, drawing interest from European, American, and Chinese actors while raising sovereignty concerns over strategic facilities.

frictionVectors.title: External-finance dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt, tourism, and imported energy leave Cabo Verde vulnerable to shocks and give development partners significant influence over infrastructure and economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and LNG leverage
frictionVectors.details: Oil and gas infrastructure remains dependent on foreign operators, export corridors, and external financing, limiting Cameroon's control over pricing and downstream industrial gains.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone conflict
frictionVectors.details: Persistent violence in the Northwest and Southwest damages transport, agricultural production, and public legitimacy while complicating outside investment in roads, plantations, and energy assets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign security-for-resources model
frictionVectors.details: The government's reliance on Russian-linked security personnel has strengthened regime protection but increased concerns over preferential access to gold, diamonds, timber, and other strategic resources.

frictionVectors.title: Transport isolation
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on corridors through Cameroon and neighboring states gives external partners substantial leverage over fuel, humanitarian supplies, and mineral exports.

frictionVectors.title: Oil revenue and pipeline dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal sovereignty remains tied to oil production and the export route through Cameroon, leaving revenue vulnerable to foreign operators, transit risks, and price volatility.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan spillover and external balancing
frictionVectors.details: The Sudan war is straining eastern border security and refugee capacity, while N'Djamena balances relations with France, the United Arab Emirates, Russia, and other competing security partners.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and French sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to contest French control of Mayotte, limiting bilateral trust and complicating migration management across the archipelago.

frictionVectors.title: Dependence on external finance
frictionVectors.details: Infrastructure and public finances remain reliant on remittances, Gulf partners, France, and other external donors, constraining autonomous development choices.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and copper competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms retain major positions in mining and processing while the United States and Europe seek alternative critical-mineral access, increasing pressure on Kinshasa's bargaining strategy.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and regional intervention
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in North and South Kivu, including alleged Rwandan support for M23, continues to undermine state control over territory, trade routes, and mineral production.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign participation in offshore oil and related services remains central to state revenues, leaving Brazzaville exposed to price cycles and limited domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, rail, and industrial projects expand connectivity but have increased concerns over debt sustainability, contract transparency, and strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Port and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Expansion of Abidjan's port and transport networks is strengthening national leverage, but financing and construction remain dependent on foreign capital and contractors.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa supply-chain pressure
frictionVectors.details: European traceability and deforestation rules could raise compliance costs for producers while multinational buyers retain substantial influence over pricing and processing.

frictionVectors.title: Competing port and military powers
frictionVectors.details: China, the United States, France, Japan, and other partners use Djibouti's ports and bases, generating revenue but limiting the government's room to balance external security interests.

frictionVectors.title: Ethiopian trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti remains Ethiopia's principal maritime outlet, making port revenues and transport infrastructure vulnerable to Ethiopian diversification efforts and Red Sea insecurity.

highlights: Suez and LNG remain strategic revenue anchors
Gulf and Chinese capital deepen leverage

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile water security
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose unilateral Ethiopian control over Nile flows and seeks a binding operating agreement. The dispute remains tied to broader Red Sea and Horn of Africa competition.

frictionVectors.title: External financing and asset sales
frictionVectors.details: IMF conditions, Gulf support, and Chinese investment provide liquidity while increasing outside influence over strategic assets, ports, and infrastructure.

highlights: Hydrocarbon revenues remain the state’s core lever

frictionVectors.title: Maturing oil and gas fields
frictionVectors.details: Declining output pressures Malabo to renegotiate terms with international energy firms and seek new offshore investment. Falling revenues constrain sovereign autonomy and public spending.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque external infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and energy projects remain important, but debt exposure and limited transparency complicate long-term control of strategic infrastructure.

highlights: Mining and Red Sea access remain state-controlled priorities
Strategic geography attracts Gulf and regional competition

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining concessions
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide hard currency but expose Eritrea to disputes over labor, revenue sharing, and concession terms. State control remains strong but economically narrow.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea military access
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea’s coastline attracts interest from Gulf and other external powers seeking naval or logistics access. Such ties can generate revenue while reducing policy flexibility.

highlights: South African corridors underpin economic security
SACU revenues remain a vital sovereignty buffer

frictionVectors.title: Dependence on South African logistics
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on South African roads, ports, electricity links, and markets. Disruptions or policy shifts in Pretoria can quickly affect national resource and trade security.

frictionVectors.title: External market concentration
frictionVectors.details: Sugar, textiles, and manufacturing depend on preferential access to regional and overseas markets. This limits diversification and leaves sovereignty partly exposed to trade-policy changes.

highlights: GERD strengthens control over future power exports
Debt and internal conflict constrain strategic autonomy

frictionVectors.title: GERD and regional water diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: The dam offers Ethiopia greater control over electricity generation and export potential but remains a major source of tension with Egypt and Sudan. Disputes over filling and operations continue to carry escalation risks.

frictionVectors.title: Debt restructuring and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt negotiations and reliance on foreign lenders shape Ethiopia’s fiscal space and infrastructure choices. Chinese-built transport and energy networks remain strategically useful but create long-term financing exposure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign concession renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Libreville is pressing foreign mining and oil operators for greater local processing, state participation, and fiscal returns. This risks friction with established French, Chinese, and other commercial partners.

frictionVectors.title: Rail and export bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on aging rail and port infrastructure limits Gabon's ability to capture more value from manganese and timber. External financiers and operators retain significant influence over logistics.

highlights: Port and fisheries sovereignty under pressure

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese transport dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegalese territory, corridors, and markets for trade connectivity. Border, transit, and customs disruptions can quickly constrain national economic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries enforcement gap
frictionVectors.details: Foreign industrial fleets and weak monitoring threaten coastal fisheries, a core food and livelihood resource. Limited patrol capacity leaves Banjul dependent on external assistance and regional cooperation.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and water security
frictionVectors.details: Illegal gold mining continues to damage rivers, farmland, and public trust despite stronger enforcement pledges. The issue pits local economic survival against environmental sovereignty and formal-sector mining interests.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and external policy constraints
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed fiscal reforms and debt restructuring limit Accra's room to redirect mineral and cocoa revenues toward domestic priorities. Foreign creditors and mining investors remain influential in economic policymaking.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou external control
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore corridor depends on multinational consortia, Chinese-linked capital, and large rail and port systems. Guinea's challenge is converting unprecedented export potential into durable domestic industrial value.

frictionVectors.title: Political legitimacy and resource concentration
frictionVectors.details: The military government's centralization of mining decisions has increased state leverage but heightened uncertainty over elections, contracts, and local consent. Political instability could invite greater external bargaining pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Guinea-Bissau exports most cashews with limited processing capacity, leaving farmers and the state exposed to foreign buyers and volatile prices. Attempts to increase local value addition remain constrained by weak infrastructure and finance.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and maritime control
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and limited maritime enforcement erode control over valuable coastal resources. External partners provide essential monitoring and budget support, but this also constrains independent policy choices.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Repayment pressures linked to major transport projects continue to constrain Nairobi's bargaining position. Control and financing of Mombasa and Lamu corridors remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: IMF-linked austerity backlash
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal consolidation and tax reforms demanded by international lenders have fueled domestic protests. Public resistance limits the government's room to trade revenue concessions for external financing.

highlights: Water exports deepen dependence on Pretoria

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water transfers to South Africa provide essential revenue but reinforce structural dependence on Pretoria. Construction delays, financing arrangements, and downstream control remain politically contentious.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining concentration
frictionVectors.details: Diamond production is dominated by foreign capital and vulnerable to commodity-price swings. Limited domestic processing reduces Lesotho's ability to capture full value from its mineral resources.

highlights: Iron ore concessions dominate the export base

frictionVectors.title: Mining concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, gold, and other mining projects are largely structured around foreign operators and external demand. Contract transparency, local employment, and revenue capture remain recurring pressure points.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Control of Buchanan and Monrovia-linked transport infrastructure is strategically important to mining companies and international partners. Liberia must balance concession investment against risks of excessive foreign leverage.

highlights: Foreign security patrons shape energy access

frictionVectors.title: Competing control of oil infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to contest terminals, fields, and state institutions around the National Oil Corporation. Production remains vulnerable to blockades and factional bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: Turkish and Russian strategic footholds
frictionVectors.details: External military and political support has entrenched foreign influence over Libya's security environment and key corridors. This complicates unified control of energy assets and limits sovereign decision-making.

highlights: Mining enclaves outpace domestic value capture

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-led mineral projects
frictionVectors.details: Large nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mining operations remain heavily dependent on foreign capital and export markets. Environmental disputes and limited local processing continue to challenge resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-access bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Roads, ports, energy, and telecommunications projects rely substantially on external lenders and investors. Financing needs can give foreign partners disproportionate influence over strategic corridors and land-use decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-sector dependency
frictionVectors.details: Foreign capital and operators remain central to developing Malawi’s uranium, rare-earth, and niobium prospects, limiting domestic value capture. Regulatory capacity and contract transparency remain key sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and logistics vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Power shortages, fuel-import dependence, and weak transport links raise exposure to external lenders and regional corridors. Fiscal stress further reduces the government’s bargaining room.

highlights: Gold and security ties shift toward Russia

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is pursuing a larger state share and tighter control over industrial gold, but relies heavily on foreign firms, equipment, and expertise. Disputes over licenses and operating conditions could deter investment or intensify informal extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Security cooperation with Russian-linked forces provides regime support but increases political and financial dependence on an external power. Persistent jihadist violence continues to undermine control over mining regions and transport routes.

frictionVectors.title: GTA gas governance
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers major export and fiscal gains, but cross-border revenue management and local-content expectations remain politically sensitive. Offshore infrastructure also depends on foreign operators and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and hydrogen exposure
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore railways, ports, and prospective green-hydrogen projects require large external investments. This creates opportunities for sovereign upgrading while exposing Mauritania to lender, off-taker, and geopolitical pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos sovereignty and basing
frictionVectors.details: The Chagos settlement and future arrangements around Diego Garcia remain central to Mauritius’s sovereignty and maritime-security posture. The issue places Port Louis between its territorial claims and the strategic requirements of the United Kingdom and United States.

frictionVectors.title: External economic concentration
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius retains strong regulatory capacity but remains exposed to foreign investment, tourism cycles, and imported energy and food. Its financial and port sectors must balance openness with safeguards against external capture.

highlights: Phosphate and renewables reinforce strategic autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate, fisheries, and infrastructure in Western Sahara remain tied to Morocco’s sovereignty claims and attract legal and diplomatic contestation. Recognition shifts and foreign investment can strengthen Rabat while provoking regional opposition.

frictionVectors.title: Water and energy exposure
frictionVectors.details: Desalination and renewable expansion improve resilience, but Morocco still faces severe water stress and dependence on imported hydrocarbons and technology. Large infrastructure programs require sustained external finance and foreign partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled LNG Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: International energy firms retain decisive control over liquefied natural gas financing, technology, and market access. Delays and security costs limit Mozambique's near-term ability to convert gas wealth into sovereign fiscal capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence continues to constrain investment and state access in the gas-producing north. Reliance on Rwandan and regional forces exposes a persistent gap in Mozambique's independent security capacity.

frictionVectors.title: External Competition for Uranium and Lithium
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, European, and other foreign investors are competing for strategic minerals and energy projects. Namibia is seeking greater local processing and fiscal participation, but infrastructure and capital dependence limit bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Infrastructure Gap
frictionVectors.details: Large hydrogen ambitions depend on foreign technology, concessional finance, export terminals, and transmission investment. Execution risks could leave Namibia supplying low-value inputs rather than retaining substantial downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Oil Export Disruption
frictionVectors.details: The junta is asserting stronger control over uranium, oil, and mining arrangements while relations with former Western partners deteriorate. Border closures, sanctions legacies, and transport insecurity reduce the practical value of that sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Greater reliance on Russian-linked security assistance provides regime protection but may trade Western influence for opaque military and resource relationships. Persistent jihadist violence continues to undermine state control outside major urban centers.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Production-Sharing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria remains dependent on international operators, lenders, and technical partners to sustain upstream production and deepwater investment. Contract uncertainty and weak regulatory credibility constrain the state's share of value.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Theft and Grid Fragility
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, sabotage, and unreliable power infrastructure continue to erode public revenue and industrial competitiveness. The Dangote refinery improves domestic leverage, but feedstock, logistics, and foreign-exchange constraints remain significant.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-Linked Mineral Scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's mineral trading and export networks face sustained international scrutiny over alleged links to armed-group economies in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Diplomatic pressure threatens market access and complicates Kigali's sovereignty narrative.

frictionVectors.title: External Security and Aid Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda converts disciplined security forces and regional deployments into political leverage, but relies on external aid, investment, and partner financing. This creates exposure to sanctions, donor conditionality, and reputational costs.

highlights: Maritime security is a national priority

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE EXPLORATION UNCERTAINTY
frictionVectors.details: Sao Tome and Principe is seeking hydrocarbon investment while avoiding overdependence on unproven offshore reserves. Foreign operators and licensing terms remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: GULF OF GUINEA FISHERIES
frictionVectors.details: Illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing by distant-water fleets threatens local revenues and food security. Limited surveillance capacity leaves the country's maritime jurisdiction dependent on external cooperation.

highlights: New oil and gas era tests resource nationalism

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON CONTRACTS
frictionVectors.details: Senegal is pushing for greater domestic value capture from new offshore oil and gas projects while relying on foreign technical and financial partners. Renegotiation pressures risk investor uncertainty and project delays.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND LOGISTICS DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Dakar's strategic transport role attracts Gulf, European, Chinese and Turkish involvement. Infrastructure financing and concession structures remain sensitive sovereignty issues amid fiscal stress.

frictionVectors.title: EXCLUSIVE ECONOMIC ZONE SURVEILLANCE
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles has significant maritime responsibilities but limited capacity to monitor its vast exclusive economic zone. Fisheries enforcement and maritime security therefore rely on partnerships with India, France and other external actors.

frictionVectors.title: STRATEGIC PORT COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The country's location draws interest from India, China, Gulf states and Western partners. Port access, infrastructure finance and military- or dual-use concerns require careful diplomatic balancing.

highlights: Mining remains central to export sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONCESSION DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, bauxite and gold production depend heavily on foreign capital, technology and export infrastructure. Weak bargaining power and limited domestic processing constrain value retention.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR FINANCING
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, road and logistics projects can improve connectivity but may deepen dependence on external lenders and operators. Contract transparency and local-content rules remain key sovereignty concerns.

highlights: Maritime resources meet fragile state capacity

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE OIL LICENSING
frictionVectors.details: Somalia is seeking offshore petroleum investment while federal and regional authorities contest licensing, revenue sharing and jurisdiction. Foreign operators and advisers are central to development, limiting near-term domestic control.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN SECURITY FOOTPRINT
frictionVectors.details: Counterterrorism, piracy prevention and maritime protection depend on multiple external security partners. This support helps preserve state authority but complicates autonomous control over ports, airspace and offshore resources.

frictionVectors.title: GRID AND PORT BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and fragile freight corridors constrain domestic control over mining value chains. Foreign investors and trading houses retain significant leverage through financing, offtake agreements, and logistics.

frictionVectors.title: MINERALS COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Competing external powers are courting South Africa over manganese, platinum-group metals, and other strategic minerals. Pretoria is seeking beneficiation and industrial partnerships without becoming dependent on any single bloc.

frictionVectors.title: PIPELINE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on Sudanese export infrastructure, leaving oil revenues exposed to conflict, transit disruptions, and bargaining by external operators. Production and public finances remain highly vulnerable to pipeline insecurity.

frictionVectors.title: ELITE AND FOREIGN RENT-SEEKING
frictionVectors.details: Armed and political elites compete over oil access, customs, and aid flows, while regional actors retain influence through security and commercial networks. Limited state capacity prevents effective national capture of resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD ECONOMY AND ARMED CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling finance rival power centers, with external buyers and regional networks extracting value outside transparent state channels. Control of mines and trade routes is closely tied to battlefield influence.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND TRANSIT COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Sudan's Red Sea coast and export corridors attract competing regional and international interests while the civil war disrupts infrastructure. Any external security or port arrangement risks deepening fragmentation of sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: LNG NEGOTIATIONS
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is pursuing long-delayed liquefied natural gas development while pressing for stronger domestic participation and fiscal returns. Large foreign capital requirements still give international energy firms substantial negotiating leverage.

frictionVectors.title: CORRIDOR AND MINING FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Rail, port, and critical-mineral projects are drawing financing from China, Gulf states, and Western partners. Diversification improves bargaining power, but debt, concession terms, and local-content enforcement remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé strengthens Togo's regional influence but relies on foreign shipping, terminal, and logistics capital. External operators retain leverage over trade flows and infrastructure standards.

frictionVectors.title: PHOSPHATE AND SECURITY PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Togo is seeking greater value from phosphate resources while managing investment and governance constraints. Spillover insecurity from the Sahel increases dependence on foreign security cooperation and can disrupt northern infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing leverage
frictionVectors.details: European funding, trade access, and migration cooperation give outside partners significant influence over Tunisian economic and security decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Imported energy vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on imported gas and hydrocarbons exposes Tunisia to price shocks and limits the benefits of its own renewable-energy potential.

highlights: Oil development advances under state direction

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and sanctions pressure
frictionVectors.details: The oil pipeline and associated projects promise state revenue but face environmental, legal, and financing pressure from Western governments and civil-society groups.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure debt concentration
frictionVectors.details: Chinese participation in roads, energy, and industrial projects expands Uganda's infrastructure capacity while increasing dependence on external lenders and contractors.

highlights: Debt relief opens room for industrial policy

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of copper value chains
frictionVectors.details: International mining firms remain central to production, processing, and investment, limiting Zambia's ability to capture full downstream value despite stronger negotiating ambitions.

frictionVectors.title: Power shortages constrain mineral expansion
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower volatility and drought-driven electricity deficits threaten mining output and force greater reliance on regional imports and private generation.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese dominance in mining finance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain prominent in lithium, platinum, and other mineral projects, providing capital and market access while raising concerns about contract transparency and local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and currency instability
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions, restricted financing, and persistent currency instability increase dependence on politically aligned external partners and complicate sovereign resource planning.
